content.headline: Israeli strike hits Gaza hospital, killing at least six, officials say
content.shortHeadline: Strike hits Gaza hospital, killing at least six, officials say
content.standfirst: Gaza’s civil defence agency says the strike hit Nasser Hospital’s surgery department in Khan Younis, killing at least six and wounding about 20. The Israeli military had not immediately commented, and the BBC says it cannot independently verify the account.

image.caption: Palestinian Civil Defence members inspect damage at Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis.

sources.originalTitle: Israeli strike on Nasser Hospital kills at least six, Gaza civil defence agency says

segments.body: An Israeli airstrike hit a building at Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza, killing at least six people and injuring at least 20, according to Mahmoud Basal, a spokesperson for the Hamas-run civil defence agency. He said the strike hit the hospital’s surgery department. A surgeon was among those reported killed.

segments.title: What is known
segments.body: The Israeli military had not immediately responded to the report. The BBC says it has contacted the Israel Defense Forces but cannot independently verify details from inside Gaza. The agency reporting the casualties operates under the Hamas-run interior ministry.

segments.title: A fragile ceasefire
segments.body: The strike comes amid continued Israeli strikes despite an October 2025 ceasefire. Gaza’s health ministry says more than 1,600 people have been killed since it began; Israel and Hamas accuse each other of violating the agreement. Heavy rain has also flooded tents sheltering displaced families, the report says.

content.headline: Scott Colom wins historic Mississippi Senate race for Democrats
content.shortHeadline: Scott Colom wins historic Mississippi Senate race
content.standfirst: Colom’s narrow victory ends Mississippi’s decades-long Republican Senate winning streak and makes him the state’s first Black senator elected since 1875. His win also adds to a strong set of Democratic midterm results.

image.caption: Scott Colom in Jackson, Mississippi, on 3 November 2026.

sources.originalTitle: Democrat Scott Colom seals historic win in Mississippi Senate race
Democrat Scott Colom unseats Cindy Hyde-Smith in stunning Mississippi Senate win
Valgsejren udbygges i USA: Nattens resultat er 'måske den allerstørste overraskelse'
How Scott Colom won deep-red Mississippi with little help from Democrats

segments.body: Democrat Scott Colom has defeated Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi’s US Senate race. With 49.2% of the vote to Hyde-Smith’s 48.7%, Colom won by fewer than 5,000 votes out of nearly a million counted. Hyde-Smith conceded and said she respected voters’ decision.

segments.title: A historic result
segments.body: Colom is the first Black person elected to the Senate from Mississippi since 1875, during Reconstruction. The state had not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982. The close result took days to resolve as counties counted outstanding ballots.

segments.title: How Colom campaigned
segments.body: Colom, a local prosecutor, campaigned across all 82 counties, focusing on voters’ concerns about costs and making direct visits to communities. The Guardian reports that he built momentum with limited early help from national Democrats, who increased their support late in the race.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s account focuses on Colom’s year-long local campaign: he spoke with voters in everyday settings and used the post-election count to draw attention to local people and businesses.

content.headline: Three men charged in US over alleged Iran-backed plots, including RAF Fairford
content.shortHeadline: Three men charged over alleged plots targeting UK and US
content.standfirst: US prosecutors accuse three men of coordinating nearly 20 attacks in Europe and the US, including an attempted attack on RAF Fairford. The charges allege links to Iran-aligned groups; the claims have not been tested in court.

image.caption: RAF Fairford, named as a target in the alleged plot.

sources.originalTitle: Three charged in US with ‘plotting Iran-backed terror attacks’ on the UK

segments.body: Three men have been charged in the US with allegedly helping to orchestrate nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks in Europe and the United States on behalf of an Iran-aligned network, according to an indictment. Prosecutors allege the network had links to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Hezbollah.

segments.title: The alleged UK links
segments.body: One alleged target was RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire. Five British men were arrested near the base in September and released on bail; a sixth British-Iranian man was also arrested later. UK counter-terrorism police said at the time they were keeping an open mind about whether anyone may have been acting for a foreign state.

content.headline: Climate analysis puts warming at 2.7C under current policies
content.shortHeadline: Current policies point to 2.7C of global warming, analysis finds
content.standfirst: A new Climate Action Tracker assessment says current policies put the world on course for 2.7C of warming by the end of the century, far beyond the Paris Agreement’s 1.5C threshold. Even meeting all national pledges would leave warming at about 1.9C.

image.caption: The 2025 Palisades fire in Los Angeles.

sources.originalTitle: World heading for ‘irrevocable overshoot’ of global temperature thresholds, analysis warns

segments.body: The world is on course to warm by 2.7C by the end of the century under current policies, according to an analysis by Climate Action Tracker. That is up from its 2.6C estimate last year and well beyond the 1.5C limit agreed by countries under the Paris Agreement.

segments.title: Pledges and progress
segments.body: Even if countries delivered all their existing pledges and long-term targets, the analysis projects warming of about 1.9C. The report notes some signs of progress: investment in clean energy is now twice that in fossil fuels, electric-car use is increasing and deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon has fallen sharply.

segments.title: A warning against giving up
segments.body: Climate Action Tracker’s chief executive, Bill Hare, says passing 1.5C must not be used to justify inaction: each additional rise in temperature matters. The analysis says several countries, including the US, Canada and New Zealand, are slowing climate action.

content.headline: Nvidia board reportedly weighs Jensen Huang’s future after new affair report
content.shortHeadline: Nvidia board weighs Huang’s future after second affair report
content.standfirst: Nvidia’s board is reportedly considering whether to remove its chief executive after reports of a second alleged affair. The company has commissioned an independent investigation into a separate reported relationship with a woman US officials believed to be a Chinese intelligence asset; the allegations remain disputed.

image.caption: Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang.

sources.originalTitle: What we know as pressure builds on embattled Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
Nvidia hires leading US law firm to investigate Jensen Huang’s relationship
Spionaffære afslører, at AI-giganters største styrke også er deres største risiko

segments.body: Nvidia’s board was reportedly meeting to consider Jensen Huang’s future after US media reported a second alleged extramarital relationship, this time with a company executive who reports to him. Nvidia has not commented on the reports. The company’s shares fell after the latest coverage, then recovered during Wednesday trading.

segments.title: An investigation, and unanswered questions
segments.body: Nvidia has hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to investigate reports about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, who US intelligence officials reportedly believed was a Chinese spy. Nvidia has said Huang will continue leading the company during the investigation. China has rejected the spying allegations as groundless, and the reporting says it remains unclear what information, if any, was gathered.

segments.title: The risks of a company built around one leader
segments.body: Huang co-founded Nvidia and has led it since 1993. TV 2’s analysis highlights how much strategy and investor confidence may depend on him, and notes that the company has no obvious successor. The board has previously expressed confidence in Huang and his leadership team.

perspectives.body: TV 2 focuses on the company’s reliance on Huang, describing a leadership structure in which many senior figures report directly to him and warning that such concentration can leave a company vulnerable if its central figure departs.

content.headline: Nigeria’s Tinubu launches re-election plan amid cost-of-living pressure
content.shortHeadline: Nigeria’s Tinubu launches re-election manifesto amid hardship
content.standfirst: President Bola Tinubu’s party has set out targets for growth, housing and security ahead of Nigeria’s January 2027 election. Analysts say the government must show households relief after reforms that have curbed inflation but driven up living costs.

image.caption: Nigeria’s President Bola Tinubu faces re-election amid continuing cost-of-living concerns.

sources.originalTitle: Nigeria's president launches re-election manifesto but can he regain voters' trust?

segments.body: Nigeria’s governing All Progressives Congress has launched President Bola Tinubu’s re-election manifesto, promising 6% annual economic growth by 2031, 200,000 affordable homes and additional security personnel. Tinubu faces an election in January 2027, with Peter Obi and former vice-president Atiku Abubakar among his challengers.

segments.title: Reforms and household costs
segments.body: Tinubu’s first-term reforms included removing fuel subsidies and changing foreign-exchange rules. Inflation fell to 14% in September 2026 from a peak of 34% in 2024, but analysts say many families still struggle with the cost of essentials. Imported rice, for example, rose sharply in price between 2023 and 2025, according to analysis cited by the BBC.

segments.title: Promises meet practical constraints
segments.body: Analysts say the manifesto’s targets depend on tackling insecurity, improving electricity supply and finding the money for investment. Tinubu proposes recruiting more military and police personnel, but one analyst says security in northern Nigeria is more complex than simply adding troops; much of the country’s farming is concentrated there.

content.headline: Tamil Nadu court orders probe into suspected AI-generated library books
content.shortHeadline: Indian court orders probe into disputed library books
content.standfirst: A court in Tamil Nadu has ordered an anti-corruption investigation into hundreds of books bought for a new public library, amid claims of false information and questionable authorship. It remains unclear whether AI was used to produce any of them.

image.caption: The newly opened Periyar Arivulagam library in Coimbatore, at the centre of the investigation.

sources.originalTitle: New Indian mega library rocked by scandal over 'AI-generated books'

segments.body: The Madras High Court has ordered an investigation into purchases for the Periyar Arivulagam library in Coimbatore, after writer Perumal Murugan raised concerns about books with unfamiliar authors, questionable ISBNs and possible false information. The state’s anti-corruption agency is investigating, and bank accounts linked to a publisher accused of supplying books have been frozen.

segments.title: What remains unknown
segments.body: The Tamil Nadu government has ordered an audit of library collections across the state. Officials say books have been removed from the new library and from Chennai’s Connemara Public Library. Although the dispute has been described by a minister as a possible AI scam, the report says it is not yet clear whether AI generated any of the disputed books.

segments.title: Questions over oversight
segments.body: More than 160 writers, researchers, artists and publishers have called for an independent inquiry, public procurement records and an audit. The controversy also has a political dimension: the state government blames the previous administration, which rejects the allegations as politically motivated.

content.headline: Spain strike protests housing costs as clashes break out in Barcelona
content.shortHeadline: Barcelona clashes follow Spain strike over housing costs
content.standfirst: Tens of thousands joined Spain’s first general strike in 14 years, with clashes between masked groups and police in Barcelona and disruption to transport and public services. The protests come less than three weeks before a parliamentary election.

image.caption: Protesters and police clash in Barcelona during Spain’s general strike.

sources.originalTitle: Clashes erupt in Barcelona after thousands join Spain general strike

segments.body: Clashes broke out in Barcelona after a general strike over housing costs and the cost of living. The BBC reports that masked men set bins alight and smashed shop windows as police used tear gas. The interior ministry said dozens of people were arrested; protests and disruption were also reported in other cities.

segments.title: A dispute over participation
segments.body: Organisers said the strike had massive support, while the business association CEOE argued it was political and not a labour dispute. About 120,000 people joined a Madrid demonstration and more than 50,000 turned out in Barcelona, according to figures cited by the BBC.

segments.title: Housing before the election
segments.body: The strike was called less than three weeks before Spain’s parliamentary election. Protesters cited unaffordable housing and rising living costs; the BBC reports that average rent for a 50-square-metre flat in Madrid was €1,170 in October, nearly half Spain’s average gross monthly salary.

content.headline: Senior US soldier arrested in UK over alleged Russia-related espionage
content.shortHeadline: US Army soldier arrested in UK over alleged espionage
content.standfirst: A 41-year-old US service member is in custody after an arrest in Gloucestershire under the National Security Act, UK police say. The FBI describes the case as involving allegations related to Russia; investigators say their inquiry is ongoing.

image.caption: Imjin Barracks in Gloucestershire, where the US soldier is reported to have been arrested.

sources.originalTitle: What we know as member of US Army arrested over ‘allegations of espionage’

segments.body: A 41-year-old US Army service member has been arrested in Gloucestershire on suspicion of offences under the National Security Act, including obtaining or disclosing protected information and assisting a foreign intelligence service. He remains in custody, and police are searching two locations.

segments.title: What authorities have said
segments.body: FBI director Kash Patel said the case involves espionage allegations related to Russia. UK Counter Terrorism Policing says the investigation is ongoing and is not linked to other active inquiries. Authorities have not announced a charge or provided further details of the allegations.

content.headline: Police watchdog warns facial recognition errors risk wrongful arrests
content.shortHeadline: Facial recognition errors could lead to wrongful arrests, watchdogs w
content.standfirst: Inspectors say officers sometimes treated retrospective facial-recognition matches as evidence without enough checks, with people from ethnic minorities at greater risk of misidentification. They call for stronger safeguards and a clearer legal framework.

image.caption: A facial-recognition search interface, illustrating concerns about accuracy and bias.

sources.originalTitle: Facial recognition errors put ethnic minorities at risk of wrongful arrest, police watchdog warns

segments.body: A report by His Majesty’s Inspectorate of Constabulary says some officers acted on potential matches from retrospective facial-recognition searches without enough corroborating checks. The results are intelligence, not proof, inspectors warn, and over-reliance could lead to people being wrongly investigated or arrested.

segments.title: Bias and safeguards
segments.body: Inspectors found that the algorithm is more likely to wrongly flag people from ethnic minorities as suspects, and that poor-quality or unsuitable images can reduce reliability. The report also found that custody images which should have been deleted were sometimes retained, and said there is no comprehensive statutory framework for the technology.

segments.title: Policing and public confidence
segments.body: The National Police Chiefs’ Council says retrospective facial recognition can help investigate crime and should be used ethically and proportionately. Inspectors say public confidence depends on human judgement, proper safeguards, stronger standards and better oversight.

content.headline: UK appoints first special representative for climate security
content.shortHeadline: UK names first climate-security representative
content.standfirst: The government is creating a role to advise on national-security risks linked to climate change, including pressures on food, infrastructure and migration. Campaigners say the appointment will need to be matched by consistent climate policy and funding.

image.caption: Prime Minister Andy Burnham arrives at Cop31 in Antalya, where the role is due to be announced.

sources.originalTitle: UK appoints world’s first special representative for climate security

segments.body: The UK has appointed Madeleine Alessandri, chair of the Joint Intelligence Committee, as its special representative for climate security. Prime Minister Andy Burnham is due to announce the role at Cop31 in Turkey. It will advise the government on climate-related security risks and work with partners in the UK and internationally.

segments.title: Risks identified
segments.body: A previously reported intelligence assessment warned that ecosystem decline overseas could create security pressures for the UK within five years, including food shortages, higher prices, migration and conflict. Alessandri says the role will strengthen understanding of climate threats and help build resilience before they develop into crises.

segments.title: Questions over credibility
segments.body: Campaigners argue the government’s actions at home must match its warnings. They point to its approval of the Jackdaw gasfield, consideration of Rosebank and possible weakening of electric-car targets. The government says it remains committed to net zero by 2050.

content.headline: Government may require entertainment industry watchdog membership
content.shortHeadline: Ministers may make entertainment watchdog membership compulsory
content.standfirst: Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy is expected to tell industry leaders to improve safeguarding or face possible government intervention, including compulsory membership of a voluntary watchdog. The move follows allegations against David Walliams, which he denies.

sources.originalTitle: Government could force media industry to improve safeguards after Walliams allegations
TV industry must tackle abuse or face crackdown, ministers warn
Author says there were 'real concerns' about David Walliams within publishing industry

segments.body: The government may require entertainment companies to join the Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority if the sector fails to improve safeguarding, the BBC reports. Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy is due to meet leaders from broadcasting, publishing, film and entertainment next week and will press them to act voluntarily first.

segments.title: A voluntary watchdog
segments.body: The standards body is currently voluntary and is intended to provide confidential whistleblowing routes and address bullying and harassment. The Guardian reports that ministers have not yet specified which organisations will attend the meeting or what changes they will be asked to make. A government official said ministers were prepared to intervene if voluntary action fell short.

segments.title: Broader calls for change
segments.body: The debate has also prompted calls to restrict the use of non-disclosure agreements in harassment cases. Allegations against Walliams were reported by the Guardian and ITV News; Walliams denies wrongdoing. The separate conviction of Russell Brand has also intensified pressure for stronger safeguards in the industry.

content.headline: Poundland seeks more time as MPs question owner’s handling of chain
content.shortHeadline: Poundland seeks rescue time as MPs criticise owner
content.standfirst: The retailer is seeking another 10 working days of legal protection from creditors while it negotiates a rescue. MPs say the owner extracted millions when the business was vulnerable; Poundland employs 12,000 people and runs 600 stores.

image.caption: A Poundland store; the retailer is seeking more time to secure a rescue deal.

sources.originalTitle: Poundland owner extracted millions when chain was on ‘knife-edge’, MPs say

segments.body: Poundland’s management will ask the High Court for a further 10 working days of protection from creditors as it seeks a rescue deal. Without the protection, the chain may have to appoint administrators. Its owner, Gordon Brothers, has released a further £10m to help the retailer buy stock and keep trading.

segments.title: Jobs and competing bids
segments.body: Poundland employs 12,000 people and operates 600 stores in the UK and Ireland. Gordon Brothers is in talks with three potential bidders but has indicated that selling the business in parts may raise more than a sale of the whole chain. The bids are reportedly worth less than the £30m in shareholder debt.

segments.title: MPs raise concerns
segments.body: The Commons business select committee questioned Gordon Brothers’ European head in private. Committee chair Liam Byrne said he was deeply concerned that the owner’s conduct may have put jobs at risk and that the company had not committed to prioritising jobs over financial returns. Gordon Brothers has said the retailer remains vulnerable to a downturn.

content.headline: UK youth benefit reform could replace £217 monthly payment with support
content.shortHeadline: Proposed youth benefit changes could replace £217 monthly payment
content.standfirst: A review due next week is expected to propose a different route for under-25s without severe work-limiting disabilities, replacing the health element of Universal Credit with employment, education and training support. Labour MPs have raised concerns about sanctions and conditionality.

image.caption: A demonstration outside Parliament against welfare benefit cuts.

sources.originalTitle: Under-25s with ADHD or anxiety set to see £217 a month disability benefits axed
Benefits cuts are looming. And Labour MPs are already threatening to rebel

segments.body: A review by youth employment chief Alan Milburn is expected to recommend a new social-security pathway for people under 25 without severe work-limiting disabilities. The i Paper reports that they could be offered education, training and employment support instead of the £217 monthly health element paid to some new Universal Credit claimants.

segments.title: A proposal, not a decision
segments.body: The review has not yet been published, and ministers have not announced a final policy. The i Paper says almost one million people aged 16 to 24 are not in education, employment or training. The proposed approach is modelled in part on systems in the Netherlands and Denmark, where support is more closely tied to participation.

segments.title: Concerns about sanctions
segments.body: Some Labour MPs are concerned that support could be made conditional on taking part in work or training, with benefits reduced for those who do not comply. The review is expected to recommend extra targeted help for vulnerable groups, including care leavers. Legislation would still need to be considered next year.

content.headline: Scottish Roman artefact points to wider imperial presence north of the Wall
content.shortHeadline: Bronze leg reshapes picture of Roman Scotland
content.standfirst: Archaeologists now believe a gilded bronze leg found in the Scottish Borders belonged to a statue of Emperor Antoninus Pius, not a monument taken from England. A new Edinburgh exhibition presents evidence of a deeper Roman presence in Scotland than previously recognised.

image.caption: Assistant curator Bethany Simpson examines the gilded bronze leg at the National Museum of Scotland.

sources.originalTitle: Bronze leg found in Scottish bog sheds new light on Roman occupation

segments.body: A bronze leg discovered in a Scottish bog in 1820 is now believed to have belonged to a large statue of Emperor Antoninus Pius erected near Hawick around AD140. Earlier antiquarians thought it had been looted from York. Archaeologists say it was carefully removed and deposited where it was found.

segments.title: A wider Roman presence
segments.body: The artefact is a centrepiece of a major exhibition opening at the National Museum of Scotland in Edinburgh. Other objects include decorated pottery and painted altars from Inveresk. Curators say the finds point to Roman occupation and influence across parts of Scotland beyond what was once assumed.

segments.title: Influence and resistance
segments.body: The exhibition also explores how Roman power shaped local politics and art. Curator Fraser Hunter says contact with Rome influenced the development of Pictish symbols, while Roman intervention helped bring larger local groups together in opposition to the empire.

content.headline: Zelenskyy leaves Denmark with new aid as Europe debates future support
content.shortHeadline: Zelenskyy leaves Denmark with 4.8bn kroner in new aid
content.standfirst: Denmark announced a further 4.8bn kroner for Ukraine during Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s visit, which also advanced discussion of a European missile-defence project. The visit comes as EU leaders disagree over how to fund Ukraine’s needs in the coming years.

image.caption: Volodymyr Zelenskyy speaks in the Danish parliament during his visit.

sources.originalTitle: Nyt våbenprojekt og et styrket Ukraine: Her er, hvad du skal tage med fra Zelenskyjs besøg
Zelenskyj rejser hjem med flere milliarder: Hvorfor skal lille Danmark bidrage mest til Ukraine?
Zelenskyjs anmodning har skabt intens debat i Europa

segments.body: Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has left Denmark after a visit that brought a new Danish aid package worth 4.8bn kroner. The donation takes Denmark’s total support to more than 90bn kroner, according to DR. The visit also included discussion of a planned European missile-defence project known as Freyja.

segments.title: A defence partnership
segments.body: DR’s defence correspondent says the project aims to create an alternative to the US Patriot missile system, while giving Denmark and NATO access to Ukrainian experience in developing weapons. The visit also included meetings with Nordic leaders and a pledge of further cooperation in defence production.

segments.title: Uneven support across Europe
segments.body: TV 2 reports that Zelenskyy has sought much larger sums from international partners as Ukraine faces a budget shortfall. EU leaders are divided over further support, with Denmark among the largest contributors relative to the size of its economy.

perspectives.body: TV 2’s account centres on the dispute over future European funding: Germany’s Friedrich Merz has threatened to block the EU’s next long-term budget unless support for Ukraine continues, prompting criticism from leaders in central Europe.

content.headline: Denmark proposes delaying EV tax rise as fuel-duty talks continue
content.shortHeadline: EV tax rise to be delayed as fuel-duty deal remains unsettled
content.standfirst: The government says it will propose postponing a planned rise in electric-car registration tax for 2027. A separate reported agreement to cut petrol and diesel duties by about two kroner per litre is not yet final, and talks with the Danish People’s Party continue.

image.caption: The government has proposed delaying a planned tax increase on electric cars.

sources.originalTitle: Regeringen vil aflyse planlagt stigning i afgifter på elbiler i 2027
Opsigtsvækkende aftale om billigere benzin kan være på vej, erfarer TV 2

segments.body: The government says it will propose delaying the planned 2027 increase in registration tax on electric cars by a year. The proposal would keep the current tax-free price threshold in place for longer, according to DR. The government has not yet secured parliamentary backing.

segments.title: Fuel-duty negotiations
segments.body: TV 2 reports that the government and Danish People’s Party are close to a tax agreement that would cut petrol and diesel duties by about two kroner per litre in 2027. The deal has not been finalised, and the parties are still discussing it.

segments.title: The trade-offs remain unclear
segments.body: The reported agreement could slow the phase-in of other tax cuts to help pay for lower fuel duties. The EV tax delay is also reported as part of the discussions, but the government has not confirmed the details of a final package. A lower fuel duty alongside continued EV incentives raises questions about the direction of transport policy.

content.headline: Danish MP apologises over posts targeting homes and vows to change approach
content.shortHeadline: Signe Wenneberg apologises and promises to change her posts
content.standfirst: Signe Wenneberg says she will stop posting about private homes in ways that could expose owners to criticism and apologises to people who felt targeted. Her contested post remains online, while reporting on her paid role at a demolition company has prompted further questions.

image.caption: Danish MP Signe Wenneberg, whose posts about private-house demolitions have drawn criticism.

sources.originalTitle: Wenneberg undskylder til dem, "som føler sig hængt ud" – kritiseret opslag er ikke fjernet
Signe Wenneberg ændrer taktik i sin kamp for bevaringsværdige huse
