segments.body: Danish MP Signe Wenneberg has apologised to homeowners who felt exposed by her social-media posts about demolitions and says she will not use images of private homes in the same way again. She says targeting or upsetting owners was not her intention.

segments.title: The post remains online
segments.body: Wenneberg’s post about a Klampenborg house was still visible on her social-media profiles when TV 2 checked. The homeowners dispute claims about whether building materials were reused and have reported her to police. Wenneberg says some comments were removed while she moderated large discussion threads.

segments.title: Questions about her role
segments.body: TV 2 reports that Wenneberg has been paid to sit on the board of demolition company LH Hockerup since 2024. The company’s director said it was not its role to decide whether a building should be demolished. Politicians from several parties have questioned her judgement.

content.headline: Danish teenager given suspended sentence over manipulated sexual image
content.shortHeadline: Teenager receives suspended sentence over shared sexual image
content.standfirst: A 15-year-old boy has received a 14-day suspended sentence after sharing a manipulated sexual image of a girl in an online group. The case highlights that edited images can still breach the law and have serious consequences for the person depicted.

sources.originalTitle: Det seksuelle billede skulle være en joke, men her er drengen Noah på vej i retten

segments.body: A Danish court gave a 15-year-old boy, identified by DR as Noah, a 14-day suspended prison sentence and required him to meet a municipal support worker. He admitted sending a manipulated image of a girl in eighth grade to a Snapchat group.

segments.title: A joke with consequences
segments.body: The image combined two pictures to place a penis over a girl’s mouth. Noah told DR he did not expect her to see it and had thought it would stay within the group. The court ruled that manipulated images are treated as real under the law.

segments.title: Impact beyond the case
segments.body: Red Barnet says young people depicted in sexual images can suffer damage to their self-esteem and may fear how widely the images have spread; some may lose confidence about attending school. A defence lawyers’ association has also warned that a conviction can have lasting consequences for a young person’s future.

content.headline: DR finds tickets being sold online to Denmark’s free Dyrehaven park
content.shortHeadline: Tickets sold online for free Danish park; police contacted
content.standfirst: A travel listing advertises entry to Dyrehaven north of Copenhagen, despite the park being free to visit. Denmark’s Nature Agency says the claims about paid access and fines are false and says it has contacted police.

sources.originalTitle: Det er gratis at besøge Dyrehaven. Alligevel sælger mystisk turisthjemmeside entrébilletter

segments.body: Tickets for 106 kroner are being offered online for Dyrehaven, a public nature area north of Copenhagen that is free to enter. The listing claims visitors need a ticket to use the paths and could be fined without one, DR reports.

segments.title: Authorities reject the claims
segments.body: The Nature Agency says the ticket claims are false and has contacted police because it suspects the sales may be illegal. The Christiania foundation also says it does not receive support from the seller, which lists tickets for the free-to-visit area as well.

segments.title: Who is behind the listing?
segments.body: The activity is listed under the name iziguide, with a company registered in Tbilisi, Georgia. The people behind it told DR that part of their annual revenue supports conservation and organisations linked to Christiania, but the Nature Agency and Christiania foundation say they have received no money.

content.headline: Danish climate researchers outline rising flood costs as warming increases
content.shortHeadline: Researchers detail what higher global warming could cost Denmark
content.standfirst: Researchers say greater warming could bring heavier cloudbursts, heatwaves and higher seas in Denmark. One set of estimates puts the combined present value of future storm-surge and cloudburst damage at 336bn kroner in a scenario below 3C, while adaptation could reduce flood damage substantially.

image.caption: Graphic illustrating how higher global temperatures could increase climate risks in Denmark.

sources.originalTitle: Er du hægtet af COP31? Her får du overblikket fra tre forskere

segments.body: Three climate researchers explain how higher global temperatures could affect Denmark, including more intense heatwaves, drier summer spells interrupted by heavy rain and potentially stronger storms. They stress that the impacts grow as warming increases, even though the exact future remains uncertain.

segments.title: Estimated costs and adaptation
segments.body: DTU calculations cited by DR estimate storm-surge damage at 175bn kroner and cloudburst damage at 161bn kroner in present-value terms over the next century in a scenario below 3C of warming. The researchers say 110bn kroner in adaptation investment could reduce flood damage by 70%.

segments.title: Long-term sea-level risks
segments.body: The researchers expect sea levels around Denmark to rise by roughly 50–60cm by the end of the century compared with 1980–2009, while saying higher outcomes cannot be ruled out. They describe several-metre rises over coming centuries as a long-term risk, not a precise forecast for Denmark.

content.headline: Motorway expansion between Vejle and Aarhus opens ahead of schedule
content.shortHeadline: Three-lane motorway between Vejle and Aarhus opens early
content.standfirst: The last section of the expanded motorway has opened, ending three years of roadworks and night closures along the route. The project was completed ahead of schedule and within budget, the Danish Road Directorate says.

image.caption: The expanded motorway near Ejer Bavnehøj by Skanderborg.

sources.originalTitle: Slut med kø og nattespærringer: Motorvej står klar før tid

segments.body: The final section of the motorway expansion between Vejle and Skanderborg opened overnight, completing a three-lane route in both directions from Skærup to Aarhus North. The roadworks had brought narrowed lanes, lower speed limits and night closures.

segments.title: Finished before the original plan
segments.body: The Danish Road Directorate had expected the last paving work to be completed in summer 2027. Project manager John Kjærsgaard said the work had finished early and stayed within budget, while drivers told DR they welcomed the end of the delays and the additional road space.

content.headline: Pochettino ready to accept Manchester United offer to replace Carrick
content.shortHeadline: Pochettino ready to take Manchester United job
content.standfirst: United have opened talks with the former Tottenham and Chelsea manager, who is understood to want the role. Michael Carrick’s future and any formal offer remain unresolved.

image.caption: Michael Carrick and Mauricio Pochettino, as United consider a change of manager.

sources.originalTitle: Pochettino ready to accept Man Utd offer to replace Carrick
Pochettino a decade in Man Utd's making - but Carrick deserves better

segments.body: Manchester United have opened talks with Mauricio Pochettino about replacing Michael Carrick, and sources have told BBC Sport the USA manager wants the job and would accept a formal offer. United would have to pay $10m (£7.5m) to release him from a contract signed in August.

segments.title: A long courtship, with a difficult task ahead
segments.body: Pochettino has been linked with United at several points since 2016. Phil McNulty’s analysis notes his record of building teams and developing players, but also the scale of the problems at Old Trafford and questions about how he would work with the club’s leadership.

perspectives.body: Chief football writer Phil McNulty sees Pochettino as a potential middle ground between sentimental appointments and short-term fixes. He also warns that United’s troubled squad and years of poor decisions would make the job a formidable rebuilding challenge.

content.headline: Harry Kane poised to become England men’s most-capped player against Croatia
content.shortHeadline: Kane poised to set England men's appearance record
content.standfirst: Kane is set to win his 126th England cap at Wembley, moving past Peter Shilton’s record of 125. The milestone follows a career in which he has become his country’s record goalscorer and captain.

image.caption: Harry Kane, who is set to become England’s most-capped men’s player.

sources.originalTitle: Leader, role model, extraordinary - how Kane's 'fairytale' came true

segments.body: Harry Kane is set to become the most-capped England men’s player when the team meet Croatia at Wembley on Thursday. The Bayern Munich striker has 125 appearances and 91 goals; goalkeeper Peter Shilton held the previous appearance record with 125 caps.

segments.title: From debut goal to captain
segments.body: Kane scored 79 seconds into his England debut in 2015. He has since captained the side 97 times and appeared in 36 major-tournament matches, more than any other England player. He says he is focused on the team rather than the personal milestone.

content.headline: Andreeva wins 11 games in a row to reach WTA Finals semi-finals
content.shortHeadline: Andreeva storms past Sabalenka to reach WTA Finals last four
content.standfirst: Mirra Andreeva recovered from 4-1 down in the first set to beat Aryna Sabalenka 6-4 6-0 and advance as group winner. Elina Svitolina also kept her hopes alive with a comeback win.

image.caption: Mirra Andreeva, who beat Aryna Sabalenka to reach the WTA Finals semi-finals.

sources.originalTitle: Andreeva wins 11 games in a row to thrash Sabalenka at WTA Finals

segments.body: Andreeva won 11 games in a row to defeat world number two Sabalenka and reach the last four at the WTA Finals. After falling behind 4-1, the French Open champion took advantage of an erratic display from Sabalenka and won 6-4 6-0.

segments.title: Svitolina stays in contention
segments.body: Elina Svitolina came back from a set down to beat Wimbledon runner-up Karolina Muchova 3-6 6-2 6-2, keeping her title hopes alive. In Stockholm, Denmark’s Holger Rune reached the quarter-finals in his return from an Achilles injury.

content.headline: Murphy beats O’Sullivan 4-0 as world champion Wu also exits
content.shortHeadline: O’Sullivan and world champion Wu both lose
content.standfirst: Shaun Murphy swept past Ronnie O’Sullivan at the Champion of Champions, while Wu Yize was knocked out by Chang Bingyu. Murphy later beat Chang 6-0 to reach the semi-finals.

image.caption: Ronnie O’Sullivan, who was beaten 4-0 by Shaun Murphy.

sources.originalTitle: O'Sullivan and world champion Wu both lose

segments.body: Ronnie O’Sullivan lost 4-0 to Shaun Murphy in Leicester, extending a difficult run of form. Wu Yize, the reigning world champion, was also eliminated, losing 4-3 to compatriot Chang Bingyu after Chang recovered from a 3-1 deficit.
Murphy then beat Chang 6-0, making breaks of 50, 142, 107, 78 and 70 to reach the last four without dropping a frame. Neil Robertson and Chris Wakelin had already secured semi-final places.

content.headline: Eddie Jones wants Japan to unsettle England at Twickenham
content.shortHeadline: Jones urges Japan to bring chaos against England
content.standfirst: Japan coach Eddie Jones says his side will try to disrupt England and turn the crowd against them, taking inspiration from Italy’s first win over England. He also praised Steve Borthwick.

image.caption: Eddie Jones and Steve Borthwick, who have previously worked together.

sources.originalTitle: Japan want 'the sky to fall in' at Twickenham - Jones

segments.body: Japan coach Eddie Jones says his team will try to create “havoc” and “chaos” when they face England on Saturday, hoping to make the home crowd uneasy. Japan have lost all six previous Tests against England, but Jones points to Italy’s first win over them earlier this year as inspiration.

Jones described Japan as “massive underdogs” but said England could be distracted by the prospect of facing New Zealand next week. He also called Borthwick an outstanding coach, after England’s 45-22 win over Australia eased pressure on the head coach.

content.headline: Bethell ruled out of England’s Australia tour and doubtful for South Africa
content.shortHeadline: Bethell out of Australia tour and doubtful for South Africa
content.standfirst: A recurrence of Jacob Bethell’s knee problem has ended his hopes of playing in England’s white-ball series in Australia and puts his place on the Test tour of South Africa in doubt.

image.caption: Jacob Bethell, who has been ruled out of England’s Australia tour.

sources.originalTitle: Bethell out of Australia trip and doubt for SA

segments.body: Jacob Bethell will miss England’s white-ball tour of Australia after a setback in training. The 23-year-old, who has not played for England since July, had surgery in September and travelled to Australia hoping to return. He is now due to go home for a specialist assessment.

segments.title: Test place now uncertain
segments.body: Bethell is a major doubt for England’s Test tour of South Africa, which begins on 17 December. His 154 in the final Test against Australia in January was one of the few highlights of that Ashes series. England have called up James Coles as white-ball cover; Bethell’s recovery timeline is not yet known.

content.headline: MP calls for legal limits on repetitive heading in football training
content.shortHeadline: MP urges legal limits on football heading in training
content.standfirst: Labour MP Grahame Morris has called for enforceable safeguards against repeated heading in training, citing concerns about brain injury. Existing football guidance is voluntary, and the proposal is not law.

image.caption: Football guidance already limits heading in training in England and Scotland.

sources.originalTitle: Legally restrict heading a football in training, says MP

segments.body: Morris has submitted an Early Day Motion urging the government to limit repetitive heading in training and develop enforceable safeguards. Researchers have found footballers are three and a half times more likely to die from a neurodegenerative disease than the general population.

segments.title: Guidance already exists
segments.body: In England, guidance recommends no more than 10 headers a week in amateur training and limits high-force headers for professional players. Scotland also bans heading in professional training on the day before and after matches. Head Safe Football founder Judith Gates argues voluntary rules are not enough; the FA says the evidence on long-term brain health remains under study.

content.headline: England cancel women’s West Indies Test to prepare for Ashes at home
content.shortHeadline: England replace Windies Test with Ashes preparation
content.standfirst: England will play four red-ball matches in the UK ahead of next summer’s Women’s Ashes Test, rather than the scheduled Test in the West Indies. The ECB says the change is a performance decision.

image.caption: Sophie Ecclestone, who has taken five-wicket hauls in her last two Tests.

sources.originalTitle: England cancel Windies Test in favour of home Ashes warm-ups

segments.body: England have removed the scheduled April Test in the West Indies from their tour and will instead play three T20s and three one-day internationals there. The decision is not related to financial discussions between the ECB and Cricket West Indies, according to BBC Sport.

segments.title: More red-ball cricket before Australia
segments.body: Nat Sciver-Brunt’s team will play three intra-squad matches and a three-day fixture against Australia A before the Ashes Test at Headingley, scheduled for 24-27 June. They will also hold a red-ball training camp in India in January. West Indies have not played a women’s Test since 2004.

content.headline: Cristale’s debut mixtape brings every side of the Brixton rapper into view
content.shortHeadline: Cristale puts her full story into her debut mixtape
content.standfirst: After weighing paths from football to university, the Brixton-raised rapper has finished her first full-length project. Clear Intentions ranges across grime, hip-hop and R&B, without guest artists to tell her story for her.

image.caption: UK rapper Cristale.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Young, Black and female in Brixton is hard’: ​from football to Top Boy and wordplay, the inspiring journey of UK rapper Cristale

segments.body: Cristale’s Clear Intentions is the 25-year-old rapper’s first completed full-length project, after two earlier attempts. The Brixton-raised artist says she made the mixtape a personal “mental audit”, drawing on relationships with herself, family, friends and work. She chose not to include guest artists: “I don’t feel like I need help telling this part of my story.”

segments.title: A path of her own
segments.body: Football, drawing and an architectural-design degree were among the possibilities Cristale considered before she committed to music. She says she faced assumptions about what a young Black woman from Brixton could achieve, while her parents encouraged her early recordings. Her sound has since expanded from drill to include grime, melodic guitar, hip-hop and R&B.

content.headline: Jane Wiedlin’s candid memoir revisits the Go-Go’s, fame and a difficult life
content.shortHeadline: Jane Wiedlin tells the story behind the Go-Go’s hits
content.standfirst: The Go-Go’s songwriter reflects on the pressures of fame, sexism in the music business and living with bipolar disorder. Her new memoir also describes painful experiences she says shaped her life and relationships.

image.caption: Jane Wiedlin.

sources.originalTitle: ‘My partners would all tell you I was a nut job’: Jane Wiedlin on the Go-Go’s, fame and the freedom of sex dungeons

segments.body: In TMI, Jane Wiedlin writes about the Go-Go’s and the life behind their bright power-pop hits. The band became the first all-female group to play its own instruments and write its own material to reach No 1 on the US album chart; Wiedlin says she wanted to tell her story without making herself look good or avoiding difficult subjects.

segments.title: Fame and its costs
segments.body: Wiedlin recalls that the band was often dismissed or sexualised by the music press, and says sexism shaped the way the Go-Go’s were treated. She also speaks about depression and bipolar disorder, and says she was diagnosed with bipolar disorder at 58. Her account includes an allegation that she was sexually assaulted as a minor by Rodney Bingenheimer; the Guardian says attempts to reach him for comment received no response.

content.headline: U2’s Carnaval de Luz finds the band sounding renewed and ready to reconnect
content.shortHeadline: U2 return to loud guitars on a newly confident album
content.standfirst: Their first album of new songs in almost nine years brings Larry Mullen Jr back to the drums and reaches for a more joyful, expansive sound. The band discuss how their shared decision-making shaped the record.

sources.originalTitle: U2: Carnaval de Luz review – rousing, restorative rock from a band ready to take on the world again
‘It’s a new world. It’s a little fascistic. And it needs a different response’: U2 on 50 years together – and why Bono can’t work with Trump

segments.body: U2’s Carnaval de Luz is their first album of new songs in almost nine years. The review hears a band revitalised by Larry Mullen Jr’s return to the drum kit, with loud guitars, spiritual themes and a renewed sense of purpose. It praises standout songs including “Street of Dreams” and “If the World Is at War We Better Not Be”, while noting that some lyrics retain Bono’s familiar earnestness.

segments.title: A band built on compromise
segments.body: In a separate interview, U2 describe their shared songwriting credits and committee-style decisions as a form of band democracy. They also discuss why Bono does not feel equipped to negotiate with the Trump administration, and say they still believe rock music can bring people together.

content.headline: Jorge Drexler’s journey from doctor to Oscar-winning songwriter
content.shortHeadline: Jorge Drexler finds freedom in music, movement and candombe
content.standfirst: The Uruguayan musician says it took decades to shake off the effects of growing up under a dictatorship that discouraged artistic expression. His new album returns to the candombe sound of home.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I didn’t dance until I was 45’: how Jorge Drexler went from repressed doctor to rump-shaking Oscar-winner

segments.body: Jorge Drexler trained as a doctor and began writing songs while working in medicine, before building a career as a singer-songwriter in Madrid. His song for The Motorcycle Diaries won the Academy Award for best original song in 2005, though he was not invited to perform at the ceremony. He sang it there anyway, delivering an a cappella version in place of an acceptance speech.

segments.title: Finding his rhythm
segments.body: Drexler says he grew up in Montevideo during a dictatorship hostile to musicians and artists, and “didn’t dance” until he was 45. His album Taracá returns to the candombe music of Uruguay and was nominated for eight Latin Grammys ahead of the awards on 12 November. He says the success of Spanish-language artists is widening the music’s reach.

content.headline: Sufjan Stevens gathers a sprawling history of Christmas songs into one set
content.shortHeadline: Sufjan Stevens’ Christmas songs find warmth in a new collection
content.standfirst: This compilation draws mostly on the singer-songwriter’s earlier holiday releases, with one new song. The review finds some odd choices but hears a consoling, communal spirit in the collection.

sources.originalTitle: Worst Christmas Ever!

segments.body: Worst Christmas Ever! collects songs from Sufjan Stevens’ earlier Christmas releases, adding one new track, “This Christmas (It Only Gets Better)”. The review questions some selections, including novelty treatments of “Holly Jolly Christmas” and “It Came Upon a Midnight Clear”, but finds the compilation’s strongest moments in the more intimate songs and their layered voices.

segments.title: A hand held out
segments.body: The new song’s lyrics admit to misanthropy before reaching towards hope: Stevens asks whether things will get worse, then suggests the Earth might improve. The review places the release in the context of his gradual return to public activity after the death of his partner, Evans Richardson, and his diagnosis of Guillain-Barré syndrome in 2023.

content.headline: Daine’s debut album turns a tangled industry story into fizzing pop
content.shortHeadline: Daine’s debut leaps between synth-pop, emo and alt-rock
content.standfirst: The Australian musician’s first album shifts between bright hooks and noisy, unsettled textures. The review finds flashes of emotional clarity amid a sound that keeps trying on new forms.

sources.originalTitle: In Endless Awe & Agony

segments.body: On In Endless Awe & Agony, Filipino Australian artist daine moves between synth-pop, alt-rock and hyperpop, with distorted recordings, chopped vocals and bursts of screaming. The review hears a clear step forward from daine’s earlier emo-pop work, particularly in the energetic “Love Love (Love Love)” and “PQC”.

segments.title: Searching for a shape
segments.body: The album reflects on exploitation, public image and the cost of success, themes that follow daine’s journey through the music industry and their departure from Warner Australia. The review finds that these ideas do not always form a coherent story, and that the album’s shifting influences can obscure its own identity. “(I Want You In) Dakota” stands out for its more direct scenes of longing and uncertainty.

content.headline: Skepta turns a long-awaited album into a reflection on legacy and belonging
content.shortHeadline: Skepta’s new album traces grime’s history and his own
content.standfirst: After years of delay, The Fork and Knife brings together grime, rap and dance music in a reflection on the artist’s career and family history. The review hears a portrait of immigrant Britain as well as an account of personal growth.

sources.originalTitle: The Fork and Knife

segments.body: Skepta’s first album in seven years begins with some familiar grime and rap gestures, but gradually widens its scope. The review hears him revisit earlier parts of his career while moving between collaborations with Aya Nakamura, Central Cee, Jorja Smith and Asake, before a nine-minute cypher that puts younger MCs alongside his own established style.

segments.title: A family story in the frame
segments.body: The album’s title recalls Skepta’s grandfather, a hospitality worker who wanted a better life for his children and grandchildren. The review reads that family history alongside the artist’s public identity as a grime musician, DJ and designer, arguing that the record tells a broader story of immigrant Britain.

content.headline: Amy Winehouse’s Back to Black remains powerful on its 20th-anniversary set
content.shortHeadline: Back to Black still hits hard in its anniversary edition
content.standfirst: A new multi-disc release adds a small number of previously unheard recordings to Amy Winehouse’s landmark breakup album. The review argues that the extras illuminate its making without filling the absence left by the singer’s death.

image.caption: Amy Winehouse, whose album Back to Black is marking its 20th anniversary.

sources.originalTitle: Back to Black (20th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: The 20th-anniversary edition of Back to Black includes demos, B-sides and a live set alongside the original album. The review praises the record’s mix of 1960s-inspired arrangements and contemporary songwriting, and describes it as a defining breakup album whose personal detail and musical confidence still resonate.

segments.title: What the archive can and cannot add
segments.body: The new material traces the album’s development, including earlier versions of “Me & Mr Jones” and “Tears Dry on Their Own”. But the review notes that the set contains only five previously unheard tracks, and that the planned follow-up album’s demos were destroyed. The extras offer context, not a way to complete Winehouse’s short catalogue.

content.headline: NAZA documentary reaches more than 1.5 million viewers worldwide
content.shortHeadline: NAZA reaches 1.5 million viewers in cinemas worldwide
content.standfirst: The documentary about Israel’s surveillance of Palestinian civilians and killings in Gaza has played in 47 territories. A free global streaming release is planned for early December.

image.caption: A scene from the documentary NAZA.

sources.originalTitle: NAZA documentary on Gaza killings becomes one of year’s most watched

segments.body: NAZA, directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian, had reached 1,547,033 viewers by 6 November, according to the film’s distributor data reported by the Guardian. It has played in cinemas across 47 territories and is among the most-watched documentaries with a theatrical release in 2026.

segments.title: A broad international run
segments.body: The film has drawn particularly large audiences in Italy, where it recorded 717,517 admissions, and has also played in the UK and Ireland, the Benelux, North America, France and Germany. The Guardian says a free, multilingual global streaming release on its website is planned for early December.

content.headline: Elsinore revisits Ian Charleson’s Hamlet performed while he was dying of Aids
content.shortHeadline: Elsinore tells the story of Ian Charleson’s final Hamlet
content.standfirst: A new film starring Andrew Scott recounts the actor’s 1989 National Theatre performance. People who knew Charleson describe the physical demands of the role and correct some of the drama’s departures from their memories.

sources.originalTitle: 'A hell of a thing to take on': The moving inside story of how Ian Charleson played Hamlet on stage while dying of Aids

segments.body: In 1989 Ian Charleson took over as Hamlet at the National Theatre after Daniel Day-Lewis left the production. Charleson was living with Aids, and completed 24 performances before his final show on 13 November. The forthcoming film Elsinore, starring Andrew Scott as Charleson, retells the story of that last major stage role.

segments.title: Memory and dramatic licence
segments.body: The BBC’s interviews with Charleson’s friend Sean Mathias, fellow actor Paul Jesson and doctor Margaret Johnson describe how his illness affected the performance and how the company supported him. Johnson says she did not advise him against taking the role, unlike the doctor character portrayed in the film; Jesson recalls that Charleson was physically weaker than Scott’s portrayal suggests.

content.headline: Ron Howard’s Avedon documentary explores the photographer’s restless eye
content.shortHeadline: Avedon documentary finds the people behind the portraits
content.standfirst: The Netflix film follows Richard Avedon’s six-decade career, from fashion photography to politically engaged portraiture. Its collaborators describe how conversation and trust helped him draw out his subjects.

image.caption: A still from the documentary Avedon.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I’m looking for faces which surprise me’: how Richard Avedon photographed the soul of his subjects

segments.body: Ron Howard’s documentary Avedon follows the photographer’s work across fashion, portraiture and political projects. The film uses material from the Richard Avedon Foundation’s extensive archives, including photographs, contact sheets and recordings of conversations in his studio.

segments.title: Portraits as collaboration
segments.body: Avedon’s former assistant Sebastian Kim and producer Dallas Brennan Rexer describe a photographer who treated sitters as creative participants, using conversation and playfulness to help them relax. The review highlights his portraits of Marilyn Monroe and his work with James Baldwin on Nothing Personal, alongside the political support he quietly provided to civil-rights activists.

content.headline: Give Me the Ball! recalls Billie Jean King’s fight for equality in tennis
content.shortHeadline: Billie Jean King’s fight for equality revisited
content.standfirst: This documentary follows King’s career as a champion and advocate for equal prize money, as well as the personal challenges that became public. The review praises its lively portrait but notes a missing voice from men’s tennis.

image.caption: Billie Jean King in Give Me the Ball!

sources.originalTitle: Give Me the Ball! review – tennis trailblazer Billie Jean King is ferocious force for equality

segments.body: Give Me the Ball! revisits Billie Jean King’s rise in women’s tennis and her campaign for equal rights and prize money. It also covers the high-profile 1973 “battle of the sexes” match with Bobby Riggs and the public revelation of King’s sexuality after her former partner sued her in the 1980s.

The review describes the documentary as engaging, with King herself among its interviewees and archival footage tracing her sporting and political significance. It also notes that no male tennis player appears to discuss her influence, an absence the critic finds surprising.

content.headline: 1 in 2 turns one film-maker’s bowel cancer treatment into a plea for earlier“
content.shortHeadline: 1 in 2 urges younger people not to dismiss cancer symptoms
content.standfirst: Film-maker David Wilkinson documents his own stage four bowel cancer treatment while asking why diagnoses are increasing among younger people. The film offers no clear explanation but stresses the cost of delayed diagnosis.

image.caption: Film-maker David Wilkinson in 1 in 2.

sources.originalTitle: 1 in 2 review – compassionate film about dealing with bowel cancer is a personal plea on behalf of the young

segments.body: In 1 in 2, film-maker David Wilkinson turns the camera on his own treatment for stage four bowel cancer and speaks with younger patients and NHS professionals. He asks why a disease once associated more with older people is appearing in younger age groups; the film raises diet, lifestyle and microplastics as possibilities but says there are no clear answers.

segments.title: The risk of being dismissed
segments.body: The review highlights accounts from younger patients who say their symptoms were initially misdiagnosed or written off. Wilkinson urges people not to delay using the bowel cancer test available by post, and the critic praises the film’s compassionate approach while retaining the uncertainty around why diagnoses among younger people are rising.

content.headline: Whispers in the Woods finds quiet wonder in a French forest
content.shortHeadline: Whispers in the Woods watches wildlife through a family’s eyes
content.standfirst: Vincent Munier takes his father and teenage son into the Vosges forest, where lynx, foxes and deer emerge from the shadows. The review praises a tender, visually stylised alternative to conventional nature documentaries.

image.caption: A scene from Whispers in the Woods.

sources.originalTitle: Whispers in the Woods review – paddling in the moonlight in tender study of human-animal interaction

segments.body: In Whispers in the Woods, director Vincent Munier brings his father Michel and teenage son Simon into the Vosges forest in eastern France. The film follows Simon as his grandfather introduces him to the local ecosystem, with lynx, foxes, deer and birds appearing in the winter landscape.

Rather than explain wildlife through a stream of facts or slow-motion footage, Munier often lets animals remain indistinct shapes behind branches. Warren Ellis’s score and the forest soundscape help create what the review calls a tender sense of awe, centred on the passing of knowledge between generations.

content.headline: Female Perversions gives Tilda Swinton an unconventional early US lead
content.shortHeadline: Tilda Swinton’s early US film still feels unusual
content.standfirst: Susan Streitfeld’s experimental 1996 film casts Swinton as a lawyer whose ambitions and erotic life unsettle conventional ideas of femininity. The review finds her performance singular and the film’s mix of sex and black comedy daring.

image.caption: Tilda Swinton in Female Perversions.

sources.originalTitle: Female Perversions review – Tilda Swinton searches for erotic adventures in rework of Madame Bovary

segments.body: In Susan Streitfeld’s Female Perversions, Tilda Swinton plays Eve, a successful lawyer whose relationship with a man, attraction to women and troubled memories complicate her public composure. The film draws on Louise J Kaplan’s study of sexuality and gender, but shifts its focus to a fictional character navigating desire and ambition.

The review describes the film’s theatrical scenes of sexual yearning and black comedy as an unusually experimental US debut for Swinton. It sees her performance as a sign of a screen presence resistant to conventional Hollywood roles.

content.headline: Tinto Brass, Italian director whose erotic films became cult favourites, dies at
content.shortHeadline: Tinto Brass, director of Caligula, dies aged 93
content.standfirst: The Italian director became best known for Caligula, a controversial film whose original release was reshaped by producer Bob Guccione. A later reconstruction brought more of the work closer to Gore Vidal’s screenplay.

image.caption: Director Tinto Brass.

sources.originalTitle: Tinto Brass obituary

segments.body: Tinto Brass, the Italian director known for erotic films including Salon Kitty and Caligula, has died aged 93. He began his career making work influenced by European art cinema, then became known for films that mixed eroticism, theatrical style and provocation.

segments.title: The film that followed him
segments.body: Caligula, starring Malcolm McDowell, Helen Mirren, Peter O’Toole and John Gielgud, was altered with additional scenes by co-producer Bob Guccione. Brass and screenwriter Gore Vidal asked to have their names removed from the credits. A 2023 version assembled from archival footage removed Guccione’s material and sought to move closer to Vidal’s original script.

content.headline: Walliams documentary lays out women’s allegations as Jonathan Ross responds
content.shortHeadline: Walliams allegations revisited in ITV documentary
content.standfirst: A Guardian and ITV News investigation is accompanied by a documentary featuring women’s accounts of alleged grooming and inappropriate behaviour. David Walliams denies wrongdoing; Jonathan Ross says he was unaware of the conduct alleged.

image.caption: David Walliams in 2024.

sources.originalTitle: David Walliams: Power and Silence review – some of this footage will make your head spin
Jonathan Ross ‘horrified’ by David Walliams and Russell Brand revelations

segments.body: The ITVX documentary Power and Silence accompanies a three-year investigation by the Guardian and ITV News into allegations by multiple women that David Walliams pursued them when they were teenagers or young adults and behaved inappropriately. Walliams denies the allegations, including sexual harassment and workplace misconduct.

segments.title: Responses and consequences
segments.body: Jonathan Ross has said he was “genuinely unaware” of Walliams’s conduct, despite making a 2004 joke about the comedian going home with a 15-year-old. Ross says he believed the line referred to Walliams’s publicly reported dating history and calls it tasteless. The reporting also records professional consequences, including the BBC reviewing its material featuring Walliams and Sky dropping the licence for a film he wrote and starred in.

content.headline: Rivals’ return brings grief and consequence beneath the lavish romp
content.shortHeadline: Rivals finds poignancy amid the sex and scandal
content.standfirst: The second half of the drama’s latest season keeps its outrageous romances and rivalries, but the review finds more lasting consequences and moments of grief than before.

image.caption: Aidan Turner, Catriona Chandler and Danny Dyer in Rivals.

sources.originalTitle: Rivals review – this TV joy is so much more than just a romp

segments.body: Rivals returns after Monica’s death, with the competition between Corinium and Venturer continuing alongside affairs, betrayals and family entanglements. The review says the familiar comic excess remains, but the new episodes give more weight to the consequences of characters’ choices.

segments.title: A darker turn
segments.body: David Tennant’s Tony becomes more volatile as he grieves, while the review singles out Monica’s death scene as a moment of genuine heartbreak. It argues that the series is more than a romp, though the accumulation of grief sometimes dims the fun that made it distinctive.

content.headline: The Rings of Power’s third season adds romance but still struggles to engage
content.shortHeadline: The Rings of Power adds spectacle but remains a slog
content.standfirst: A five-year time jump brings Gandalf, the forged rings and new characters further into the story. The review welcomes the added action and romance but questions whether the fantasy prequel can win back viewers.

image.caption: Jamie Campbell Bower as Celeborn and Morfydd Clark as Galadriel in The Rings of Power.

sources.originalTitle: The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power season three review – this dull show’s revamp is too little, too late

segments.body: The third season of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power picks up after the fall of Eregion, with Sauron building his power and other peoples of Middle-earth scattered across different fronts. Gandalf is more prominent, the rings are in play and the Harfoots have been sidelined.

segments.title: A relaunch under pressure
segments.body: The review sees the season as a soft relaunch, adding action, new characters and a romance between Galadriel and Celeborn. It finds the world-building and production design impressive but says the many separated plotlines still make the show feel closed-off and dramatically dull to viewers who are not already invested in Tolkien’s world.

content.headline: Inside the TV writers’ room, where collaboration and conflict shape a series
content.shortHeadline: TV writers’ rooms turn collaboration into story
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s film critic reflects on co-writing a new thriller and asks established showrunners how a writers’ room works. They describe a process that can be energising, competitive and difficult to lead.

image.caption: A scene from Hunting Alice Bell.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Like leading brave soldiers to certain death’: Succession’s Jesse Armstrong and more on the rollercoaster of TV writers’ rooms

segments.body: Writing for television can begin in a room where a team maps out plot beats and character arcs before individual writers draft episodes. The Guardian critic describes joining the room for Hunting Alice Bell, a Channel 4 thriller about a sports-centre manager targeted by online accusations and digital mob rule.

segments.title: The showrunner’s call
segments.body: Jesse Armstrong, creator of Succession, says a room can feel full of promise but can become dispiriting when a story stalls. He describes the showrunner’s responsibility to decide which direction to pursue. Other writers in the piece say rooms can range from supportive collaboration to competitive environments where writers feel they must fight to contribute.

content.headline: Manhood asks what a penis-enlargement clinic can—and cannot—fix
content.shortHeadline: Manhood looks beyond penis enlargement to men’s insecurities
content.standfirst: Daniel Lombroso’s documentary follows patients at a Dallas clinic offering injections to increase penis girth. The review finds stories of trauma, shame and self-image beneath the procedure, without a simple answer.

image.caption: David Smith, one of the patients in Manhood.

sources.originalTitle: Manhood review – a mind-boggling visit to the penis enlargement doctor who promises ‘better sex than ever’

segments.body: Manhood follows men seeking PhalloFill injections at a Dallas clinic run by Bill Moore. The treatment uses hyaluronic acid to increase girth, but the review finds the film more interested in what patients hope it will change about their lives than in the procedure itself.

segments.title: More than a cosmetic fix
segments.body: The film’s patients speak about porn, body image, shame and sexuality. The review describes Ruben’s account of childhood sexual assault as a turning point in understanding his story, and notes that another patient came to Moore after a previous enlargement procedure left him with hard lumps. It concludes that the problems explored in the film are more complex than a cosmetic treatment can solve.

content.headline: Black Doves’ cast and creator discuss the spy drama’s violent moral grey areas
content.shortHeadline: Black Doves pairs spy-thriller violence with human drama
content.standfirst: Keira Knightley, Ambika Mod and creator Joe Barton discuss a new season that sends its agents into further danger. They explain how humour and intimate character moments complicate the show’s gleeful violence.

image.caption: Keira Knightley as Helen Webb in Black Doves.

sources.originalTitle: Keira Knightley on Black Doves: ‘The violence is like a video game’

segments.body: Black Doves returns with Helen Webb, played by Keira Knightley, facing more dangerous missions after her husband becomes prime minister. Her handler Elizabeth Reed is missing, while hitman Sam must work through a kill list. Ambika Mod joins as rogue agent Laila Joshi, a reluctant ally to Helen.

segments.title: Making violence matter
segments.body: Knightley describes the show’s action as almost video-game-like, but says Joe Barton’s writing can bring an individual death into focus and make it disturbing. Barton says audiences are accustomed to violence in spy stories; the series tries to acknowledge that moral grey area while keeping its compromised characters compelling.

content.headline: Maya Jama’s next move tests whether television can still make a presenter
content.shortHeadline: Maya Jama leaves Love Island for a new Netflix chapter
content.standfirst: After leaving Love Island and signing a Netflix deal, Jama has a larger audience and a less certain path. The i Paper’s analysis argues that the presenter’s next challenge is finding a new format to make her own.

image.caption: Maya Jama, who has announced she is leaving Love Island.

sources.originalTitle: Maya Jama belongs to a dying breed of presenters

segments.body: Maya Jama is leaving Love Island after nine series across four years and has signed a deal with Netflix, which says projects are in development. Her recent appearance on Celebrity Traitors reached a wider audience than the start of this year’s Love Island, according to the commentary.

segments.title: Finding a format
segments.body: The piece argues that traditional television offers fewer established programmes for a new presenter to inherit, while launching an original format has become difficult. It suggests Netflix may give Jama room to build a programme around her own style, but notes that details of the deal have not yet been announced.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s future is uncertain after the Disney+ partnership ends
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who faces an uncertain future off screen
content.standfirst: The BBC has ended its Disney+ collaboration, cancelled a planned Christmas special and is seeking a new production partner. Fans and writers debate what went wrong—and what the long-running series needs next.

image.caption: Several actors who have played the Doctor, including Peter Capaldi, David Tennant, Ncuti Gatwa and Jodie Whittaker.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: After Ncuti Gatwa’s run as the Fifteenth Doctor ended in 2025, the BBC and Disney+ partnership has been discontinued. The BBC cancelled a planned Christmas special and is seeking another company to help fund future production, but no new partner or Doctor has been announced.

segments.title: A changing institution
segments.body: The article traces the programme’s earlier cancellation in 1989 and revival in 2005, then considers recent criticism of its scripts, casting and direction. Lifelong fan Frank Skinner says he worries the show has been kept off air for too long; former writer Nina Metivier points to kindness and curiosity as core values worth preserving. The future remains unresolved.

content.headline: Grand Theft Auto’s cultural reach goes far beyond crime and car chases
content.shortHeadline: How Grand Theft Auto became a cultural colossus
content.standfirst: As GTA VI approaches, a feature traces how Rockstar built detailed, satirical worlds from film, music and city life. A companion look at the series’ movie influences shows how it has borrowed from—and fed back into—popular culture.

image.caption: Lucia and Jason, the protagonists of Grand Theft Auto VI.

sources.originalTitle: Crime pays: how Grand Theft Auto became a cultural colossus
‘It’s so glossy and sexy!’: 10 movies (and one TV show) that inspired Grand Theft Auto

segments.body: Grand Theft Auto grew from a 1997 game about stealing cars in imagined US cities into a vast open-world series. The feature argues that its cultural reach comes not only from crime and cinematic references, but from the freedom to inhabit densely observed cities and discover incidental details between missions.

segments.title: A dialogue with film
segments.body: A related feature traces influences including Scarface, Miami Vice, Goodfellas, Boyz n the Hood and Bonnie and Clyde. It also describes the traffic in influence running both ways: Rockstar has drawn on film and television, while later filmmakers have reflected the series’ own style and imagery.

content.headline: Ocarina of Time’s remake delights, and its midnight launch brings fans together
content.shortHeadline: Ocarina of Time remake revives a shared gaming ritual
content.standfirst: The Switch 2 remake updates a landmark Zelda game while preserving its melancholy, according to the review. A separate report from London’s midnight launch finds the appeal of meeting fellow fans—and the frustration of a long queue.

image.caption: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2.

sources.originalTitle: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time review – a dream come true
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has revived the midnight game launch – but was it worth the wait?

segments.body: The Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time keeps the original game’s world, puzzles and story structure while adding voiced scenes, expanded dialogue, updated controls and an orchestral score. The review praises the result as a reinvention that makes the 1998 game feel vivid without losing its melancholy.

segments.title: A night in the queue
segments.body: At a London midnight launch, hundreds of fans waited for early copies and exclusive collectibles. The Guardian’s reporter describes the shared excitement of the gathering, but also the disappointment of a queue that moved so slowly that some customers left their details to receive the promised box by post.

content.headline: Can Alex Garland make Elden Ring work as a Hollywood fantasy film?
content.shortHeadline: Elden Ring adaptation faces a formidable challenge
content.standfirst: The game’s scale, horror and sparse storytelling make it a difficult world to translate for film. The project is reportedly shot and in post-production, but its budget and distribution plans remain uncertain.

image.caption: Elden Ring.

sources.originalTitle: Alex Garland’s Elden Ring adaptation is on course to be Hollywood’s goriest ever fantasy movie

segments.body: Alex Garland’s adaptation of Elden Ring is in post-production, according to the article, with a cast including Cailee Spaeny, Ben Whishaw and Nick Offerman. The game has sold more than 30 million copies and is widely regarded as a major work of fantasy, raising expectations for a film that must make its world matter to viewers unfamiliar with the game.

segments.title: A world without easy answers
segments.body: The feature argues that Elden Ring’s grotesque creatures, sprawling mythology and bleak tone pose a different challenge from more conventional fantasy adaptations. It says a reported budget near $200m could leave Garland less room for the ambiguity found in earlier films, while the movie’s plot and final form remain unknown.

content.headline: Blood test signal may reveal ovarian precancer before tumours form
content.shortHeadline: Blood signal may detect ovarian precancer before tumours form
content.standfirst: A study found that levels of an RNA molecule in blood could help identify a precursor to ovarian cancer. The result is promising, but the research does not establish a screening test for general use.

sources.originalTitle: Molecular signal in blood helps detect early risk for ovarian cancer, study finds

segments.body: The study examined Tu-Stroma, an RNA molecule found at higher levels in the blood of women with serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma (STIC), a precancerous condition that can precede ovarian cancer. Researchers detected STIC in 92.3% of affected women and correctly identified 98.2% of healthy women in their study.

segments.title: What the results could mean
segments.body: For women with inherited risk factors, the researchers reported that about 72% of positive results would be accurate, while nearly 100% of negative results would be correct. A blood test that could indicate whether precancerous lesions are present might eventually inform difficult decisions about preventive surgery. Its performance and usefulness in wider clinical practice remain to be established.

content.headline: New obesity criteria could correct millions of BMI diagnoses
content.shortHeadline: A broader obesity test could correct millions of BMI diagnoses
content.standfirst: An analysis of health records suggests BMI alone can miss excess body fat or label some people incorrectly. The proposed approach adds body measurements and checks whether fat is affecting organ function.

sources.originalTitle: BMI alternative for identifying obesity ‘could prevent misdiagnosis in millions’

segments.body: An analysis of records from more than 800,000 people in the UK, US, China and Spain suggests that BMI alone misses obesity in 5–9% of adults and wrongly diagnoses it in as many as 3%. The proposed approach combines BMI with waist measurements or waist-to-height ratio to assess excess body fat.

segments.title: Risk is not the same as disease
segments.body: The approach also distinguishes clinical obesity, where excess body fat is already impairing organ function, from pre-clinical obesity, where it presents a risk but has not yet caused those problems. The researchers report that 80–90% of people with pre-clinical obesity did not progress to clinical obesity over the following 10 years. The method is more involved for clinicians, and the article does not establish how widely it will be adopted.

content.headline: Small baxdrostat follow-up hints at lasting effect on some hypertension
content.shortHeadline: Small study hints baxdrostat’s blood-pressure effect may last
content.standfirst: In a follow-up involving 14 patients, blood pressure stayed lower for up to two years after they stopped the drug. Researchers say a larger study is needed before claiming a limited course can provide a lasting cure.

sources.originalTitle: New drug that could permanently cure high blood pressure coming to UK by 2027

segments.body: Baxdrostat is designed to block production of aldosterone, a hormone that can raise blood pressure. An analysis following 14 patients from a larger trial found that their blood pressure remained lower for up to two years after they stopped taking the drug, following six to 12 months of treatment.

segments.title: A finding still to prove
segments.body: The researchers suggest the drug may affect cells that overproduce aldosterone in some people with benign adrenal tumours. The small follow-up does not prove a permanent cure: one researcher said a larger study now under way is needed to establish whether the effect lasts. The drug’s UK availability and NHS use are also not settled in the report.

content.headline: US tests autonomous mine-hunting systems as Gulf shipping faces risk
content.shortHeadline: Autonomous systems take on mine-hunting as Gulf shipping faces risk
content.standfirst: Robotic boats and underwater vehicles can search for mines while keeping sailors farther from danger. They can reduce risk, experts say, but cannot prove that a route is clear.

sources.originalTitle: Robot vessels take on the dangerous work of mine hunting

segments.body: Mine-hunting has traditionally relied on specialist ships and crews. Newer systems, monitored by people on shore, use sonar and sensors to search the seabed; some build three-dimensional images that software can analyse for objects resembling mines. The latest Gulf conflict is providing a test for more capable US systems, though the military has disclosed limited details.

segments.title: Reducing, not removing, risk
segments.body: Uncrewed systems can keep sailors out of immediate danger and may be deployed with smaller teams. But, as a former Royal Navy robotics officer put it, operators “can't prove the negative” that no mines are present; they can only reduce the risk. The report says the US considers the Omani route cleared and that shipments are running at about 75% of pre-conflict levels, while uncertainty about the threat remains.

content.headline: Germany reportedly bars Chinese drones from military sites over security fears
content.shortHeadline: Germany reportedly bans Chinese drones at military sites
content.standfirst: Reports say Germany is withdrawing commercially available Chinese-made drones from military bases and training grounds. The move reflects wider security concerns, but the reporting identifies no specific threat from the drones.

sources.originalTitle: Germany reportedly bans Chinese drones at military bases over security concerns

segments.body: Germany has reportedly banned Chinese-made commercial drones from military bases and training grounds, with units told to withdraw them as quickly as possible. Der Spiegel reported that individual military units had bought drones, including models from DJI, with limited oversight and no central record of purchases.

segments.title: Concern without a named threat
segments.body: The report places the move alongside other restrictions and warnings about connected vehicles and devices, based on fears that sensors could expose sensitive information. US military officials have not identified a specific threat in the cited vehicle case. BYD, responding to concerns about its cars, says data processed or stored by its vehicles cannot be remotely accessed from China.

content.headline: UK under-16 social media rules could reach YouTube Kids and Spotify
content.shortHeadline: Proposed UK rules could put YouTube Kids and Spotify in scope
content.standfirst: The UK government is considering a broad definition of platforms that could bring services not usually thought of as social media within an under-16 ban. The final scope and exemptions are not yet settled.

sources.originalTitle: UK social media ban expansion for under-16s could cover YouTube Kids

segments.body: Draft rules could bring as many as 150 platforms into the UK’s under-16 social media ban, according to sources briefed on the proposals. Services potentially affected include YouTube Kids, Spotify and Lego Play, because the government is considering recommender systems and user-generated content as part of its approach.

segments.title: Scope and an possible exit
segments.body: The government had said educational, shopping and music-streaming services would be exempt, but industry representatives say a broad test leaves platforms unsure whether they would be covered. Ministers say services could fall outside the rules if they remove harmful features, although companies argue that removing recommendation systems could undermine how their services work. The regulations are still under consideration.

content.headline: AI data-centre plans could add vast gas capacity as UK sites face local disputes
content.shortHeadline: AI data centres could drive major gas buildout and local opposition
content.standfirst: A BloombergNEF analysis says planned on-site gas plants could add 181GW of capacity across the US and Europe as data centres wait for grid connections. A proposed east London campus shows how the expansion is also colliding with local concerns.

image.caption: Fields proposed for a data-centre campus in North Ockendon, east London.

sources.originalTitle: AI datacentres plan on-site power stations on huge scale despite climate risks, research reveals
'We all need data, but do we need the largest data centre in Europe here?'

segments.body: Data-centre projects in the US, UK and mainland Europe have proposed 181GW of on-site gas-fired capacity, according to BloombergNEF, citing delays to grid connections. If built, the planned capacity would emit an estimated 345 million tonnes of carbon-dioxide equivalent annually in the US, where 90% of the on-site gas plants are proposed. The report warns that facilities described as temporary could keep generating power after grid connections arrive.

segments.title: A local test of the expansion
segments.body: In North Ockendon, east London, developers Digital Reef have proposed a large data-centre campus on green-belt land. Local residents raise concerns about construction, noise and pressure on electricity and water supplies. The developer says the project would bring jobs and public green space; a London planning report identifies grid capacity and water use as constraints on growth. The proposal has not yet been approved.

content.headline: AI use puts university coursework under pressure as regulator urges exams
content.shortHeadline: Regulator urges more exams as AI challenges university assessment
content.standfirst: England’s higher education regulator says some students can complete assessments with AI in minutes and evade detection. Universities are changing how they grade work, while student representatives argue that traditional methods also need reform.

sources.originalTitle: AI has made it ‘close to impossible’ to assess university coursework, regulator says
Students passing university assessments in minutes using AI, regulator warns

segments.body: Research by England’s Office for Students and Advance HE, based on interviews and surveys involving staff and students at at least 127 institutions, found that some assessments can be completed to a high standard with AI in minutes. The regulator says AI use can be difficult to detect and warns that assessments may fail to measure students’ own knowledge and skills.

segments.title: Changing how students are assessed
segments.body: The regulator points to closed-book and practical exams, in-person presentations and oral exams as ways to assess learning without relying on unsupervised written work. Universities UK says institutions are already adapting with a mix of exams, process-based work and controlled AI use. The National Union of Students argues that some traditional assessment methods are themselves outdated and should be redesigned with students.

perspectives.body: The National Union of Students says AI is exposing weaknesses in traditional learning methods, including essay questions, handouts and slideshows, and calls for innovative approaches developed with students.

content.headline: New York starts registering major AI developers under safety law
content.shortHeadline: New York opens registration for major AI developers
content.standfirst: A state safety law will require large frontier AI companies to publish safety frameworks and report critical incidents. New York has opened registration ahead of the rules taking effect at the start of 2027.

sources.originalTitle: OpenAI, Anthropic face new oversight as New York’s AI safety law takes effect

segments.body: New York has opened a registration portal for major frontier AI developers, which must register by 1 January 2027 under the RAISE Act. The law applies to companies with more than $500m in annual revenue and requires published safety frameworks, public model transparency reports and reports of critical safety incidents within 72 hours.

segments.title: Enforcement and oversight
segments.body: The state’s new Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity, and Trust will oversee the law. Penalties can reach $1m for a first violation and $3m for later violations. New York has also launched a research centre to evaluate advanced AI systems and review companies’ safety frameworks; other states have adopted or are developing similar measures.

content.headline: Tamil Nadu library investigation raises questions over alleged AI-generated book
content.shortHeadline: Tamil Nadu probes library book purchases amid AI allegations
content.standfirst: A court has ordered an investigation into disputed public-library purchases in Tamil Nadu. Writers have raised concerns about questionable authorship and errors, but it remains unclear whether AI was used to produce any of the books.

image.caption: The newly opened Periyar Arivulagam library is at the centre of the allegations.

sources.originalTitle: New Indian mega library rocked by scandal over 'AI-generated books'

segments.body: The Madras High Court has ordered an anti-corruption investigation into books bought for a new public library in Coimbatore, after novelist Perumal Murugan questioned their authorship and accuracy. The state government has ordered an audit of library collections, and officials say 523 books have been removed from Chennai’s Connemara Public Library following preliminary checks.

segments.title: What remains unproven
segments.body: The allegations have prompted scrutiny of the procurement process and concern about how libraries can verify books as AI-generated material spreads. The BBC report says it is not clear whether AI was used to create any of the disputed titles. Tamil Nadu’s government blames the previous administration for the purchases; the DMK denies wrongdoing and says the allegations are politically motivated.

content.headline: Startup bets on simulations to make AI agents more reliable
content.shortHeadline: Startup uses simulations to tackle AI-agent failures
content.standfirst: Plurai says it can test AI agents against simulated versions of a company’s systems and use the results to improve performance. The approach addresses a known reliability challenge, but the claimed gains and cost savings remain company claims.

sources.originalTitle: Plurai wants to help AI agents work better using the same approach that helped get self-driving cars to roads

segments.body: AI agents can fail on complex tasks, according to benchmarks cited in the report: one evaluation found leading systems succeeding on fewer than 83 of 100 tasks, while a simulated corporate test recorded 76.8% accuracy for its best-performing model. Startup Plurai says it is adapting techniques used to test self-driving systems to help agents handle unusual situations before they encounter them in business.

segments.title: Testing against a company’s systems
segments.body: Plurai builds a digital twin of the software, information and tools an agent would use, then maps possible task flows to identify edge cases. The startup says it can use those results to train smaller open-weight models and, in tests with Nvidia and Nebius, outperform some mid-tier frontier models at lower cost. Those results are not independent evidence of performance in wider deployment.
